# Update Windows 10 SDK to 18362.

<!-- Thank you for submitting a pull request to our repo. -->

<!-- If this is your first PR in the ASP.NET Core repo, please run through the checklist
below to ensure a smooth review and merge process for your PR. -->

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable. (I don't think this needed any).
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable. (I don't think this needed any).
- [x] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. If you'd like to propose a new feature or change, please open an issue to discuss the change or find an existing issue.

<!-- Once all that is done, you're ready to go. Open the PR with the content below. -->

This changes the Version of the Windows SDK used in the repository to 10.0.18362.0.

The WindowsVersions file under the testing/xuint was updated as well for 21H2.

## Description

~~This fixes an issue where the install Visual Studio script installs the wrong version of the Windows SDK. I decided to fix it by having both Dev16 and Dev17 to install the absolute latest stable (that I know of that is) which is 10.0.22000 and use that in place of all the other older versions. This will help new contributors later with contributing as then it is then less for them to need to install (I personally only have 1 version of the Windows SDK installed at a time and migrate all of my projects to the latest stable all the time when I find a new one was released to conserve disk space on my development pc).~~
This fixes an issue where a different version of the Windows SDK is pulled in for VS2019 vs. VS2022. With this now both of them are the same in terms of the Windows SDK requirements.

Fixes #36165
pr_comments:
I see, so that Windows SDK is not installed on the build workers. This will need to be addressed.

cc: @dougbu know who to ask about installing the 10.0.22000.0 Windows SDK before this gets merged. Having this could help simplify local building a lot by requiring less to be installed and can allow building with only Dev17 installed as well out-of-box without needing the Dev16 build tools.

1. We considered moving all requirements to `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows10SDK.18362` (which is also available in both VS 2019 and VS2022). We dropped that due to the disruption it would cause for developers building this repo using VS 2019.   Chose instead to install `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows10SDK.18362` and expect it when using VS 2022 because users were (then) just moving to the newer IDE.
2. It does **not** appear any Windows SDK is included as a required component of any workload and the BuildTools versions don't have a `NativeDesktop` workload in any case.
3. You're correct the CI agents do not include `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows10SDK.22000`. Changing that would be a disruption for the .NET Core-Eng team.

I think we're left relying on `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows10SDK.17134` for VS 2019 and `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows10SDK.18362` for VS 2022. We could reconsider if you could better describe a major upside of the `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows11SDK.22000` component. We may also make a difference choice whenever we start thinking about the VS version after VS 2022.

That said, your changes in src/Installers/Windows/AspNetCoreModule-Setup/CustomAction/aspnetcoreCA.vcxproj and src/Installers/Windows/AspNetCoreModule-Setup/build/settings/common.props highlight incorrect assumptions we should fix. Could you narrow this PR to correcting `$(PlatformToolset)` and `$(WindowsTargetPlatformVersion)` in those files, aligning with our current installation options❔

> 1. We considered moving all requirements to `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows10SDK.18362` (which is also available in both VS 2019 and VS2022). We dropped that due to the disruption it would cause for developers building this repo using VS 2019.   Chose instead to install `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows10SDK.18362` and expect it when using VS 2022 because users were (then) just moving to the newer IDE.
> 
>     2. It does **not** appear any Windows SDK is included as a required component of any workload and the BuildTools versions don't have a `NativeDesktop` workload in any case.
> 
>     3. You're correct the CI agents do not include `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows10SDK.22000`. Changing that would be a disruption for the .NET Core-Eng team.
> 
> 
> I think we're left relying on `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows10SDK.17134` for VS 2019 and `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows10SDK.18362` for VS 2022. We could reconsider if you could better describe a major upside of the `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows11SDK.22000` component. We may also make a difference choice whenever we start thinking about the VS version after VS 2022.

I consider these few as upsides:

- When the developer chooses to only use and have installed the absolute latest stable version of the Windows SDK.
- When apis need to be added to the native code that requires the latest stable version of the Windows SDK because something became a public api that was not defined in the older versions.
- When constants are changed from an older version of the Windows SDK because of an introduction of a new one so the max value of say for example a flag constant in the Windows SDK required changing as well and so it means something different on newer versions of Windows (say for example a new MiniDumpWriteDump flag was introduced for a dump type so the max value was increased). Not updating the Windows SDK and doing a Windows OS version check might introduce a bug when the code is run on the newer versions of the operating system that ships with those changes.
- Less for the developer to install with the InstallVisualStudio.ps1 script, even in VS2022 you still need the 17134 windows sdk to build the installers and so it was a pain for me to need to install VS2019 as well as that version of the windows sdk just to be able to build *everything* that can possibly be made. I would rather just install a single version of the Windows SDK and the IDE if possible (with the build tools provided with the IDE itself).

I guess another option is to have a build task that somehow looks for the latest Windows SDK the user has installed and then select that instead of forcing 17134, 18362, or even 22000 that way it's all the same version and they will be happy for it.

> That said, your changes in src/Installers/Windows/AspNetCoreModule-Setup/CustomAction/aspnetcoreCA.vcxproj and src/Installers/Windows/AspNetCoreModule-Setup/build/settings/common.props highlight incorrect assumptions we should fix. Could you narrow this PR to correcting `$(PlatformToolset)` and `$(WindowsTargetPlatformVersion)` in those files, aligning with our current installation options❔

So the common.props is imported by the vsxproj files I edited then? If so I could move the `$(WindowsTargetPlatformVersion)` to that file so then it only gets changed in that 1 spot.

@AraHaan I think I was unclear: My suggestion was to fix ~~two~~ five files where a single `$(PlatformToolset)` or `$(WindowsTargetPlatformVersion)` is currently hard-coded. That should correct your fourth bullet.

We'll discuss your broader suggestion later this week.

> I guess another option is to have a build task that somehow looks for the latest Windows SDK the user has installed and then select that instead of forcing 17134, 18362, or even 22000 that way it's all the same version and they will be happy for it.

This sounds very complicated but might be doable in a central place like eng/targets/Cpp.Common.props.

If it matters, looks like the following also have `$(PlatformToolset)` hard-coded:

- src/Installers/Windows/AspNetCoreModule-Setup/IIS-Setup/iisca/lib/iisca.vcxproj
- src/Installers/Windows/AspNetCoreModule-Setup/IIS-Setup/IIS-Common/lib/IISSetup.CommonLib.vcxproj
- src/Installers/Windows/AspNetCoreModule-Setup/IIS-Setup/IIS-Common/reftrace/reftrace.vcxproj

After looking at the components, component groups, and workloads configured for Windows build agents, we suspect `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows10SDK.17134` doesn't need to be explicitly referenced when installing VS 2019 (perhaps, as long as recommended components are brought in) and `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows10SDK.18362` doesn't need to be explicitly referenced when installing VS 2022. Might also mean the JSON files are a bit longer than necessary because they use `"includeRecommended": false`.

I'm generally leaning toward requiring `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows10SDK.18362` everywhere. That component should already be available on all build agents with VS 2019 or 2022 installed. However, such a change comes with a downside of requiring VS 2019 _users_ to manually install another optional component. Might be the right time to take that hit because we just recently had to start requiring a couple of ARM64 components.

If necessary, we could request a newer SDK be installed on build agents. That would take longer.

Thoughts @dotnet/aspnet-build❔

> I'm generally leaning toward requiring Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows10SDK.18362 everywhere. 

That seems reasonable to me.

I will need to possibly include the other files (mentioned above) as well that may need to be changed on the ``PlatformToolsetVersion`` when using the VS2022 build tools / IDE to ``v143``, else it will use ``v142`` (VS2019).
It wasn’t! MicrosoftDocs/visualstudio-docs#7538<https://github.com/MicrosoftDocs/visualstudio-docs/pull/7538>
I find it odd that it seems to ask for the 2010 build tools on the failing parts of the CI. I think there is something going wrong somewhere with that one.

~~Unrelated general point: Visual Studio's `msbuild` files may do a good job finding ~~the `$(PlatformToolset)` version matching the VS installation as well as~~ the `$(WindowsTargetPlatformVersion)` for the latest installed Windows SDK. Are our settings (which override but match those defaults) good or bad❔ I don't know the best practices here.~~

~~But, if~~ it's best practice to include those settings **and** this is great work @AraHaan.

> I find it odd that it seems to ask for the 2010 build tools on the failing parts of the CI. I think there is something going wrong somewhere with that one.

From the binary log at <https://dev.azure.com/dnceng/_apis/resources/Containers/9260680/Windows_Logs?itemPath=Windows_Logs%2FRelease%2FBuild.Installers.binlog>, looks like Platform.Defaults.props "wins". That file uses `v100` if `$(PlatformToolset)` is empty. The setting in aspnetcoreCA.vcxproj is seen later and "loses" because a value is already set.

Bottom line, please add a `$(PlatformToolsetVersion)` property in src/Installers/Windows/AspNetCoreModule-Setup/CustomAction/aspnetcoreCA.vcxproj and set `$(PlatformToolset)` unconditionally. This will match the other native projects.

> … set $(PlatformToolset) unconditionally …

Well, this certainly answers my "best practice" question about `$(PlatformToolset)` 😀

> the `$(WindowsTargetPlatformVersion)` for the latest installed Windows SDK

This was also incorrect. From the above binary log, it appears `$(_LatestWindowsTargetPlatformVersion)` (the default value of `$(WindowsTargetPlatformVersion)` is `10.0.19041.0` even though `10.0.18362.0` is installed on the VS2019 agents. So, my whole "general point" can and should be ignored.

I made this PR ready for review because I bet the current AzDO builds will succeed.

Thinking about also enabling auto-merge unless @Tratcher, @wtgodbe, or @AraHaan have objections (will wait a bit). If I do that, I'd make the consolidated commit description

So that way it's more correct with the actual changes inside.
Auto-merge now enabled.
We're well past the native / installer builds in the CI validation. It's been a long journey and I greatly appreciate you sticking with it @AraHaan. Many thanks❕❕

@dotnet/aspnet-build should we create a pinned issue to help contributors learn about newly required VS components❔ Recent changes here and in #39417 added:

- `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.VC.ATL.ARM64` aka `C++ ATL for latest v142 build tools (ARM64)` or `C++ ATL for latest v143 build tools (ARM64)`
- `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.VC.Tools.ARM64` aka `MSVC v142 - VS 2019 C++ ARM64 build tools (Latest)` or `MSVC v143 - VS 2022 C++ ARM64 build tools (Latest)`
- `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows10SDK.18362` aka `Windows 10 SDK (10.0.18362.0)` if using VS 2019

> should we create a pinned issue to help contributors learn about newly required VS components❔

That's an interesting policy question - if we do that this time we should do it every time we update requirements, which I don't think we already do (except for when we bump up the required VS version). https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/docs/BuildFromSource.md is already generic enough so as to be correct (it suggests looking at `vs.x.json` files or running `InstallVisualStudio.ps1`), so I'm leaning towards it not being necessary
Discovering these requirement changes can be a real pain, even for people on the team. We should come up with some kind of notification.

> Discovering these requirement changes can be a real pain, even for people on the team. We should come up with some kind of notification.

Perhaps make a github bot that emails the team members whenever changes like this happen so at least they *got* notified in case something happened and local builds on their end started to not work.

Hi @AraHaan. It looks like you just commented on a closed PR. The team will most probably miss it. If you'd like to bring something important up to their attention, consider filing a new issue and add enough details to build context.

> 
> * `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.VC.ATL.ARM64` aka `C++ ATL for latest v142 build tools (ARM64)` or `C++ ATL for latest v143 build tools (ARM64)`
> * `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.VC.Tools.ARM64` aka `MSVC v142 - VS 2019 C++ ARM64 build tools (Latest)` or `MSVC v143 - VS 2022 C++ ARM64 build tools (Latest)`
> * `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.Windows10SDK.18362` aka `Windows 10 SDK (10.0.18362.0)` if using VS 2019

Have you considered adding them to the [`.vsconfig`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/a899ce80c36138df814b3258093a21de3ca95c5c/.vsconfig)? That should [make VS automatically prompt for install](https://docs.microsoft.com/visualstudio/install/import-export-installation-configurations?view=vs-2022#automatically-install-missing-components).

Hi @rainersigwald. It looks like you just commented on a closed PR. The team will most probably miss it. If you'd like to bring something important up to their attention, consider filing a new issue and add enough details to build context.

> Have you considered adding them to the .vsconfig?

We have added the requirements to src\Installers\Windows\.vsconfig, src\Servers\IIS\.vsconfig, and similar files. Those files and the one in the repo root are ignored when building from the command line. We're fine on helping contributors using VS interactively but not when they only build from the command line.

issue_context.title: InstallVisualStudio.ps1 pulls wrong Windows SDK version
issue_context.body:
I believe the `InstallVisualStudio.ps1` file is supposed to bring all required components to be able to build the solution.
However when I tried to run the quarantined tests it failed with a missing Windows SDK, and wanted `10.0.18362.0` whereas the script installed `10.0.17134.0`.

I ran `& ./eng/build.ps1 -CI -nobl -all -pack -NoBuildJava` to get the error
comments:
I would rather have ASP.NET Core depend on 10.0.22000.0 where that is that latest version of the Windows SDK.

Why? Because developers like me install and use only the very latest version of the Windows SDKs and uninstall the older ones to make room for other stuff (since they are about 2~3 GB each.

It could also help out on InstallVisualStudio.ps1 as well.

See also: https://developer.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/downloads/windows-sdk/

What do you think @mkArtakMSFT?

In the mean time I made this patch locally (as well as updated all of the json files to 22000) of the sdk and everything builds without issues:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/15173749/147401060-d4996a11-4171-4902-a3f2-f1c14284fc4b.png)

However for vs2022 it seems that ``src\Installers\Windows\AspNetCoreModule-Setup\CustomAction\aspnetcoreCA.vcxproj`` needs a patch to conditionally use the ``v143`` platform toolset instead of ``v142``.

Alright going to open pull request to try to close this issue (Note: For dev16 and dev17 it will require the 10.0.22000.0 windows sdk).

If that SDK is not available on the dev16 feeds, you should still be able to access it from Dev17 at least to install it. Besides I think Dev17 at this point is required for the main branch anyway (or at least I use it with that).

Sad news, the CI on the Windows x86/x64/arm64 and the Windows Server images seems to not have 10.0.22000.0 installed on the Windows SDK so the change (that should hopefully resolve this issue) is currently blocked.

review_comments: @Tratcher do we update this file proactively i.e. before we have test code needing to distinguish new Windows versions❔ @AraHaan, if yes, we could do this part even if we rejected all the rest.
Not usually, but this is fine.
